dynamical-behavior-of-engineering-struct.caption: Figure 4a. Wavenumber against frequency for the same SAFE branches shown in Figure 4, with a logarithmic wavenumber axis in radians per metre. Select the 20 × 20 mm square bar (0 to 190 kHz), the IPE 80 I-beam (0 to 52 kHz), the 60E1 rail (0 to 22.5 kHz), the NPS 1¼ schedule 40 pipe (0 to 175 kHz) or the 10 mm plate (0 to 250 kHz), and drag the wave markers to compare their wavenumbers. Each window holds as many branches as the reference for that section: the published SAFE curves for the bar and the rail, the exact solutions for the pipe and the plate, and, for the I-beam, which has no published curves, the same model on a mesh of half the element size. Every mesh agrees with one of half its element size within 0.2%. The plate is infinite across its width, with A0 and S0 Lamb waves and SH0 shear-horizontal waves from zero frequency, and A1 and SH1 cutting on at 161 kHz. Wavenumber is computed as k = 2πf/cₚ = 2π/λ; wave packets travel at the group velocity while their crests travel at the phase velocity.

machine-learning-the-complete-picture-an.caption: Figure 2a. Three forecasting methods fitted to the same synthetic monthly sensor signal: (a) seasonal ARIMA, (b) additive Holt-Winters exponential smoothing and (c) gradient boosted trees with lagged inputs. Each method forecasts 24 months using only the history before the selected origin. Withheld observations appear after the forecasts, with RMSE and MAE measured over all 24 months. Tree forecasts recursively use their own predictions as future lag inputs. The shaded interval in (a) is the ARIMA model's 95% prediction interval. The figure steps through the forecast origins, months 120, 156 and 192, in turn; choose one to stay on it and compare different histories. The relative performance changes with the origin.

Figure 6a. Three feature-selection methods on one reproducible synthetic regression example, with 360 training rows and 120 held-out test rows. The target depends on x1 (energy), x2 (duration) and x3 (frequency); x4 is a noisy copy of x1, and x5 and x6 are nuisance inputs. (a) A Filter ranks absolute Pearson correlations and keeps three features. (b) A Wrapper adds features using five-fold cross-validation, fitting its scaler inside each fold, and keeps three: after the third feature the cross-validated error is flat. Move the step slider to inspect the candidate subsets of all six steps. (c) An Embedded method uses Lasso: increasing the L1 penalty shrinks coefficients toward zero. The dashed line marks α = 0.12. The same Ridge predictor evaluates each selected feature set on the held-out rows, which never influence selection or scaling.
